title: From Reward to Compulsion: Drugs, Learning, and Recovery
takeaways: Obtaining reward and removing withdrawal can both strengthen use; punishment, negative reinforcement, tolerance, dependence, and impaired control are different concepts.
Drug mechanisms differ before they converge.
Opioids, stimulants, nicotine, alcohol, and cannabinoids begin at different receptors, transporters, or channels even when several influence dopamine-related learning.
Places, odors, internal sensations, and stress can renew responding after the drug is absent; intoxication, withdrawal, and cue-triggered seeking require separate measurements.
Receptor location changes exposure and signaling.
Membrane entry, phosphorylation, endocytosis, recycling, and intracellular compartments determine which targets a drug reaches and how their responses change over time.
A task result requires its actual preparation.
Calcium fluorescence, movement, receptor labeling, self-administration, and clinical recovery measure different events; a cellular or animal finding is not by itself a clinical treatment outcome.

Maintenance medicines stabilize opioid exposure, rescue antagonists reverse acute toxicity, cessation and alcohol medicines target distinct mechanisms, and behavioral care changes cues, consequences, and daily functioning.
